study.title: Discordance between clinician- and patient-reported outcomes during radiotherapy for brain metastases: the prospective NeuroPRO study

cover.headline: Doctors systematically **miss symptoms** that matter most to patients with brain cancer

slides.title: If clinicians alone decide what counts as a side effect, patients suffer symptoms no one is tracking or treating.
slides.body:
This reveals a structural perception gap in neuro-oncology care. The symptoms doctors miss most are psychological distress and physical complaints not obviously tied to radiation.

Routine patient self-reports could catch what clinical exams overlook and shift care toward what patients experience.

slides.title: Across 84% of symptoms tracked, patients reported worse severity than their doctors recorded during brain radiation treatment.
slides.body:
Researchers compared clinician assessments against patient questionnaires at three points during radiotherapy for brain metastases. Agreement was fair for worry and depression but almost perfect for vomiting and seizures.

The biggest gaps appeared for shortness of breath, fatigue, and sleep trouble.

slides.title: Sixty-three patients receiving brain radiation completed questionnaires at baseline, end of treatment, and first follow-up.
slides.body:
Doctors scored side effects using standardized toxicity criteria. Patients rated the same symptoms using quality-of-life scales designed for cancer and brain tumor patients.

The study generated 4,448 matched comparisons and measured agreement for each symptom.

caveats: This study found a pattern, not a cause. Something else could explain the link between clinician assessments and patient reports.
The sample was sixty-three patients at centers participating in the study, which may not reflect all radiation oncology practices or patient populations.
Agreement varied widely by symptom type, so the overall pattern may obscure important differences in how specific side effects are perceived.

unsupported_claims.problem: The abstract specifies patients receiving radiotherapy for brain metastases. Brain metastases are secondary cancers that have spread to the brain from elsewhere, not primary brain cancer. This is a medically significant distinction.

unsupported_claims.claim: The symptoms doctors miss most are psychological distress and physical complaints not obviously tied to radiation
unsupported_claims.problem: The abstract states 'particularly within psychological domains and somatic symptoms not readily attributable to radiotherapy.' The copy changes 'not readily attributable to radiotherapy' to 'not obviously tied to radiation,' which is essentially the same meaning, but adds 'The symptoms doctors miss most' as a superlative claim. The abstract shows these had larger discrepancies but does not explicitly state these are 'most missed' in a definitive ranking.

However, the abstract does not specify this occurred 'during brain radiation treatment' - the timepoints were baseline, end of treatment, and first follow-up, so some assessments were before or after treatment, not only during.

source.abstract: Background Clinician-reported outcomes (CROs) remain a central component of side effect assessment in radiotherapy, while patient-reported outcomes (PROs) are increasingly being integrated into standard practice to better capture the subjective symptom burden experienced by patients. Agreement between CRO and PRO has not been prospectively studied in patients undergoing radiotherapy for brain metastases. Methods NeuroPRO was a prospective longitudinal cohort study enrolling patients receiving radiotherapy for brain metastases. CROs were assessed using predefined CTCAE (version 5.0) items, while PROs were collected using the EORTC QLQ-C30 and BN20 at baseline, end of treatment, and first follow-up. Upon completion of radiotherapy, decision regret was evaluated additionally using the Ottawa Decision Regret Scale. Chance-corrected agreement between CRO and PRO was quantified for each item using Gwet's second-order agreement coefficient (AC2). Longitudinal differences were additionally explored using two-way ANOVA and agreement was further characterized using Bland-Altman analyses with calculation of limits of agreement (LoA). Results Sixty-three patients were included, completing 278 questionnaires and yielding 4448 matched CRO-PRO item comparisons. Across 27 of 32 shared symptoms (84%), PRO scores were higher than CRO scores, indicating systematic symptom underestimation by clinicians. Chance-corrected agreement (Gwet's AC2) was fair to moderate for psychological and neurological symptoms (worry AC2 = 0.30; depression AC2 = 0.39; drowsiness AC2 = 0.44) and substantial to almost perfect for gastrointestinal and treatment-related symptoms (vomiting AC2 = 0.96; seizures AC2 = 0.94; nausea AC2 = 0.92), corroborating the pattern observed with mean-based comparisons. The largest single-item discrepancies were observed for dyspnea (bias 1.00; 95% LoA 0.85-1.14; group p p p Conclusion Sole clinician assessment systematically underestimates symptom burden in patients undergoing radiotherapy for brain metastases, particularly within psychological domains and somatic symptoms not readily attributable to radiotherapy. These findings reveal a structural perception gap and support the routine integration of PROs into interdisciplinary neuro-oncologic care to enhance symptom recognition and promote patient-centered management (DRKS00031480).
